title: The Tricycle, the Ice Pops and the School Shop That Became Wahaha
dek: In 1987 a 42-year-old salesman borrowed 140,000 yuan to sell ice pops and stationery to Hangzhou schoolchildren, and listened to their parents.

story.event: Taking charge of a school-run sales department in Hangzhou and selling ice pops and stationery to pupils
story.summary: In 1987, aged 42, Zong Qinghou took charge of a sales department for school-run businesses in Hangzhou's Shangcheng district, borrowed 140,000 yuan and, with two retired teachers, sold ice pops, soft drinks and stationery to pupils. After processing tonics for other firms, he noticed parents' worries about picky eaters and in 1988 launched a children's nutritional drink under the Wahaha name, which grew into one of China's largest beverage companies.
paragraphs: In 1987 Zong Qinghou was 42. He had left school after junior high to help support his family, then spent about fifteen years doing manual work in the Zhejiang countryside, including at salt mines and on tea farms, before returning to Hangzhou in 1978. For most of the next decade he sold for a factory owned by a school, buying silk in Sichuan to sell in Hangzhou and trading scarce aluminium. "My only dream at that time was to have my own company and do what I wanted to do," he later said in an oral history.

That year he was put in charge of a sales department serving the school-run businesses of the city's Shangcheng district. By his own account it came with two retired teachers and a desk. He borrowed 140,000 yuan. Riding a tricycle, he sold soft drinks, ice pops at a penny each and stationery to children at a nearby primary school, and sold ice cream on commission for a local client. He told a Wharton professor in 2005 that the first year brought in 100,000 yuan. The enterprise was collectively owned, not his; he said the state had invested nothing in it.

In the second year he moved into processing oral tonics for other companies, which he said earned more than 700,000 yuan. Then two things changed his thinking. Buyers had begun to question what was in such tonics, including whether they contained hormones. And selling door to door, he learned that many parents of only children worried about picky, poorly nourished eaters. Nothing on the market, he later said, was aimed at China's more than 300 million children. He brought in a nutrition professor and in 1988 launched a children's drink under a new name, Wahaha, roughly "laughing child", advertising heavily on Hangzhou television.

Demand soon outran the little operation. In 1989 it became the Wahaha Nutritional Food Factory, and by 1990 annual sales were close to 100 million yuan. In 1991 Wahaha, with about 100 staff, took over a loss-making state cannery with more than 2,000 workers, a move some criticised at the time. Zong built it into one of China's largest drinks companies and was its chairman when he died in February 2024, aged 79.

quote.text: such wisdom is concerned not only with universals but with particulars, which become familiar from experience, but a young man has no experience, for it is length of time that gives experience
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Aristotle explains why practical wisdom is rarely found in the young: it rests on particulars that only time makes familiar. Zong began at 42, and his decisive particulars came from years of selling: which goods moved, which ones buyers distrusted, and what parents at the door were worried about.

reflection: It is easy to count the years before a beginning as delay. Zong's account suggests something else. The ice pops and the tonics were small trades, but the rounds that carried them taught him what parents were anxious about, and that became the product.

You also carry particulars that no textbook holds: which part of a working day goes wrong when people are tired, what a colleague really needs when they ask for help, which promise a supplier tends to break. That is not a lesser kind of knowledge. It is the kind Aristotle thought only time can give, and it is worth noticing before it starts to feel too ordinary to mention.
invitation: Write down one thing you know about your work only because you have done it for years, something a newcomer would miss. Keep the note where you will see it next week.

cross_checks.claim: In 1987, aged 42, Zong borrowed 140,000 yuan to start the school-linked retail business
The business started with two retired teachers
It sold ice pops, soft drinks and stationery to schoolchildren
Zong noticed parents' worries about picky eaters and developed a children's nutritional drink with a nutrition specialist
The Wahaha children's drink was launched in 1988 and the Wahaha Nutritional Food Factory set up in 1989
Annual sales were close to 100 million yuan by 1990
In 1991 Wahaha took over a loss-making state cannery, a move criticised at the time

research_notes: First-year money: Zong told Wharton (2005) he 'made 100,000 yuan in the first year (1987)' and over 700,000 yuan in the second; The World of Chinese (2024) says 220,000 yuan profit in the first year; Yicai gives output value of 4.4 million yuan and net profit of 222,000 yuan by May 1988. The story gives Zong's own figures, attributed to him, and does not state a profit. Start-up money: CNN, Yicai and The World of Chinese say he borrowed 140,000 yuan; Fortune says his wealth began with a '$22,000 family loan'. The story says only that he borrowed 140,000 yuan and gives no lender or dollar conversion (CNN converts at the 1987 rate to about $38,000; Yicai at the 2024 rate to $19,450). Product timing: Yicai and the second Yicai piece date the children's drink to 1988; the BBC and Wharton date the Wahaha Nutritional Food Factory to 1989; The World of Chinese says the company was rebranded Wahaha in 1989 and calls 1988 the brand's founding year; the story uses 1988 for the drink and 1989 for the factory. The developer is a 'professor of nutrition' (CNN), 'a professor' (Zong), and 'a nutrition expert at a local hospital' (China Daily HK); the story says a nutrition professor. Sales: CNN gives nearly 100 million yuan in the drink's third year, Yicai an output value of 100 million yuan in 1990, The World of Chinese 98 million yuan revenue in 1990; the story says close to 100 million yuan. Cannery: Zong (Wharton) puts the acquisition in 1990; the BBC, Yicai and The World of Chinese date the merger to 1991, which the story uses. Ownership: Wharton reports Wahaha was wholly state-owned until 2000 and Zong describes it as collectively owned with no state investment; CNN calls it privately owned today. Funding is marked bootstrapped because the business was started with a loan and grew from its own earnings with no outside investors until Danone in 1996, but the editor should know it was a collective (school-run) enterprise rather than Zong's private property at the time. The tricycle comes from Yicai; the penny ice pops from CNN. Fifteen years in the countryside is Zong's figure (Wharton, China Daily HK); The World of Chinese says 14 years on a tea farm. The CNN obituary is cited from its CNN Newsource syndication on KTVZ because the cnn.com URL did not load. TMTPost's obituary (en.tmtpost.com/post/6951786) adds that the Shangcheng District Education Bureau put the department out to contract and that it was loss-making; it is not cited, and the story does not say the department was loss-making. The Aristotle passage is a general remark on practical wisdom and the young, applied here by analogy.
